title: Latency-backed Commitment (LBC): packaging & experiment for latency-guaranteed reserved GPUs with banked credits
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem: Enterprise customers negotiating Dedicated GPU contracts often care more about predictable tail latency for customer-facing inference than raw throughput. Current reserved SKU discounts are tied to committed GPU units and/or throughput bands, but lack a simple contract primitive that ties discount to an observable latency SLO and gives customers flexible burst capacity when we occasionally miss SLOs.

Proposal: Introduce a Latency-backed Commitment (LBC) product that bundles reserved GPUs with an explicit p99 latency target. Customers commit to a monthly reserved capacity (GPUs or concurrency lanes) and a p99 objective. Pricing has two components: a base reserved discount (higher than standard reserved because of the latency guarantee) and a small buffer of burst credits. If Redwood fails to meet the agreed p99 target in a billing window, we issue banked "latency credits" to the customer which can be consumed as burst capacity in the following window or converted to billing credit. Customers can opt for an autoscale policy that drains latency credits first before provisioning on-demand capacity.

Why different: This product ties the commercial incentive directly to an SLO that matters to product teams. It allows us to price-in reliability (we take on tail-risk) and gives customers operationally usable remediation (burst credits) rather than only refunds.

Scope: Design pricing tiers, contract language for security/questionnaire, technical meters for measuring p99 across customer routes, billing adjustments and UI surfaces in Console, and a staged experiment with select enterprise customers.
acceptance_criteria: Pricing matrix with at least 3 LBC tiers (conservative/high-assurance/ultra) finalized and modeled for NRR impact
Legal-approved contract appendix drafted (latency measurement, remedy options, force majeure, region failover rules)
SRE instrumentation plan implemented to calculate customer-scoped p99 correctly (route-level, model pinned, warm KV state) and exposed via Console
Billing integration to apply latency credits as burst-capacity tokens and optionally as monetary credits completed
Pilot launched with 3 enterprise customers and success metrics defined for 90-day experiment
proposed_pricing_tiers: LBC-Standard: 20% reserved discount, p99 target = 300ms, includes 10 burst-minutes per GPU per month, overage billed at on-demand rate
LBC-HighAssurance: 30% reserved discount, p99 target = 150ms, includes 30 burst-minutes per GPU per month and 5% cost-credit escrow on missed SLO windows
LBC-Ultra: 40% reserved discount, p99 target = 75ms, includes 120 burst-minutes per GPU per month, priority failover to adjacent region and 10% monetary credit on repeated misses
contract_snippet: Latency measurement: p99 is computed per invoice window on the customer-scoped API routes that are explicitly listed in Appendix A. Measurement excludes outages caused by (a) customer-managed networking, (b) customer-supplied models that fail initialization, and (c) scheduled maintenance with 72-hour notice. Remedies: For a billing window where measured p99 exceeds the target, Redwood will (i) issue X latency-credits to the customer's account (Y credits per minute of aggregate p99 overage) usable for burst capacity in the following billing window; (ii) when opted-in, convert accrued latency-credits into monetary credits at the rate described in Section 4.1. Force majeure and preemption: Redwood will not be liable for SLO breaches resulting from third-party cloud region-wide outages; in those cases Redwood will (at its discretion) provide cross-region failover within the customer's reserved bands.
rollout_plan: Week 0-2: Legal & security review for contract appendix and SQ answers
Week 2-4: SRE and runtime implement route-scoped p99 meter, unit tests and integration tests
Week 4-6: Billing and Console teams implement latency-credit bucket and UX for consumption/visibility
Week 6-8: Internal dogfood with Redwood Platform team, simulate misses and credit consumption
Week 8-12: Pilot with 3 selected enterprise accounts (1 fintech, 1 consumer-SaaS, 1 healthcare - all with NDA)
Week 12-16: Evaluate pilot, iterate pricing, legal changes, and prepare GA launch decision
experiments: A/B experiment: Offer LBC-HighAssurance to cohort A and a traditional reserved SKU + SLO-based monetary rebate to cohort B; compare churn, net revenue retention and support overhead over 90 days
Autoscale policy test: For pilot customers opt-in to 'latency-credits-first' autoscale vs 'on-demand-first' and measure cost delta and SLO compliance
Pricing sensitivity: Run price elasticity sims in sales negotiations (discount vs p99 target) and capture willingness-to-pay across 10 enterprise deals
metrics: Primary: Pilot NRR lift (delta vs baseline) after 90 days
SLO hit rate: fraction of invoice windows meeting contracted p99
Support volume: number of latency-related tickets per 1M tokens for LBC customers
Cost-to-serve: incremental GPU and routing cost attributable to burst credit redemption
Conversion rate: percent of pilots converted to annual LBC contracts
dependencies: SRE: implement and validate route-scoped p99 meters (ENG-50822)
Billing: latency-credit ledger, token issuance, redemption logic (ENG-51100)
Console: UI surfaces for credit balance and SLO dashboard (DES-1203)
Legal: contract appendix and SQ updates (PM-legal-review-2026)
Sales/AE: select pilot candidates and coordinate NDAs
risks: Measurement variance: noisy p99 computation may lead to frequent small credit issuance and customer confusion
Gaming: customers might route synthetic low-latency traffic to meet SLOs; requires guarded route definitions
Cost exposure: frequent misses could create large burst redemptions against our capacity and drive margin pressure
Support burden: new SLA semantics may increase legal and SRE on-call workload during rollout
